summary: Defines a parameter on the Content-Disposition header that marks which parts of a multipart MIME message the sender considers critical. A gateway to a less capable system can use that knowledge to handle multipart messages sensibly when it cannot deliver everything.

plainLanguage.summary: The Handling parameter lets a sender mark each MIME body part as required or optional. A gateway can drop an optional part that the receiving system cannot handle, but failure of a required part means the message has failed.

questions: what is the mime handling parameter
what is the default value of handling in content-disposition
subtitle: A Content-Disposition parameter that marks message parts as required or optional for delivery.

tldr.problem: A gateway to a less capable messaging system may be unable to deliver every part of a multipart message, and it needs to know whether a failed part matters to the sender.
tldr.mechanism: The sender marks a body part with Handling=REQUIRED or Handling=OPTIONAL. A gateway must fail delivery if a required part cannot pass, while it may silently drop an optional part.
tldr.outcome: Unmarked parts default to REQUIRED, preserving all-or-nothing behavior for older senders. RFC 3459 updates RFC 3204 and was updated by RFC 5621.

today: RFC 3459 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2003 and updates RFC 3204. It was updated by RFC 5621 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Gateways Need Criticality
sections.content:
A content gateway connects mail systems with different capabilities. It may remove parts that the receiving system cannot render or store, or reject a message the system cannot handle.

RFC 3459 lets the sender mark which body parts are critical. This helps gateways distinguish a part the sender requires from one that can be omitted, including parts added by software that the sender may not have seen.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway may need to remove content that the receiving system cannot use. The sender's marks tell it which parts can be omitted and which parts must arrive.

sections.title: The Handling Parameter
sections.content:
The sender places the Handling parameter on a body part's Content-Disposition header. Handling=REQUIRED means the sender considers that part critical; if the gateway cannot pass it, the whole message has failed.

Handling=OPTIONAL means the sender accepts that the part may be omitted. A gateway may silently delete it, and MUST NOT report delivery failure just for that optional part unless a required part also failed.

An unmarked part defaults to REQUIRED, and unknown values are treated as REQUIRED. The word REQUIRED here is a parameter value, not an RFC 2119 requirement keyword.
sections.plainLanguage: REQUIRED means the sender expects the part to arrive; OPTIONAL means the gateway may omit it. A missing or unfamiliar marking defaults to REQUIRED.

sections.title: Syntax and Case Handling
sections.content:
The parameter name is handling, and the defined values are REQUIRED and OPTIONAL. The parameter name and values are case-insensitive.

RFC 3204 registered the parameter. RFC 3459 repeats the registration and serves as a normative reference for other specifications that use Handling.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter has two defined values, and capitalization does not change their meaning. The sender adds it to a body's Content-Disposition header.

sections.title: Notifications for Failed Parts
sections.content:
The Handling value affects whether a gateway generates a delivery notification. For OPTIONAL content, the gateway MUST NOT generate a notification because that part could not be passed. For REQUIRED content, notification follows the normal request rules.

If a sender requested notification and a required part fails, the gateway MUST report failure for the whole message. A mail transfer agent generates a DSN; a user agent may generate an MDN. In the SIP case described by the RFC, a required unsupported part can produce response 415.

The Handling parameter alone does not request a notification. Normal notification rules still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: An optional part can fail without a failure notice for that part. If a required part fails, a requested notification reports failure for the whole message.

sections.title: Signed and Encrypted Messages
sections.content:
For signed content, a REQUIRED marking can express that the sender expects end-to-end signature verification. If the receiving system cannot verify the required signed content, the gateway must reject the message.

For encrypted content, a REQUIRED control part means the sender requires end-to-end encryption; a gateway must reject the message if the endpoint cannot decrypt it. If the control part is OPTIONAL, a gateway that can decrypt may forward cleartext because the sender explicitly allowed that handling.

Because unmarked parts default to REQUIRED, a sender who makes no change gets the required-content behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A required signature or encryption control part must be preserved for end-to-end checking. Marking an encryption control part optional can allow a capable gateway to decrypt the message.

sections.title: MIME Interactions and Examples
sections.content:
Handling applies to the selected alternative in multipart/alternative. Criticality affects only the outermost message level or selected alternative; indicators inside an embedded message/rfc822 are ignored.

For multipart/related, a sender can mark one related component as required and another as optional. The RFC gives a Macintosh data fork and resource fork as an example, where the document data may be critical but the resource fork can be omitted.

In a text-only messaging gateway example, required text can be delivered while an optional unsupported attachment is dropped. If no parts are marked, every part is required and an unsupported part can cause rejection.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway applies the marking at the message's outer level or selected alternative. If the sender marks nothing, the gateway treats all parts as required.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A sender can use signatures over critical-content indicators to protect their integrity. The gateway MUST honor signature processing; if it handles a required signature for an endpoint that cannot verify it, the gateway itself becomes a target for tampering.

Receivers must not treat Handling as proof of who sent a message. The parameter only expresses how the sender wants a gateway to handle parts.
sections.plainLanguage: The Handling marking is not proof of a sender's identity. Signatures can protect the marking, but a gateway that processes signed content must also be protected.
